column5: green pastures and waters under the shepherd's lead
column6: The psalm's shepherd makes the flock lie down in green pasture and leads it beside waters. It supplies the water and shepherd-led grazing scene that the commentary says is compressed into merʿā.

column5: Hebrew רֹעִי, “my shepherd,” cognate with رعي
column6: The Hebrew rōʿî belongs to the rʿh cognate family developed in the commentary for merʿā and rāʿā. The verse gives the compact title “my shepherd,” against which the page's deliberately indirect pastoral language can be assessed.

column5: Hebrew רְעוּ, “pasture the flock,” after watering
column6: Jacob tells the shepherds to water the flock and then pasture it. This nonmetaphorical cognate use joins the commentary's sequence of water, grass, animal mouth, and the act of grazing.

column5: shepherding a people with a staff
column6: The prayer asks God to shepherd his people with his staff and let the flock graze. It brings together the staff, flock, and pastoral rule that the commentary develops from Musa's staff and the merʿā root family.

column5: leader who leads out and brings in so sheep have a shepherd
column6: Moses asks for a leader who will go out and come in before the people, lead them out and bring them in, so they are not sheep without a shepherd. It tightly joins the commentary's secondary out/in sense with its leader-shepherd sense.

column5: rain in season and earth yielding produce
column6: God promises rain in its season, the land's yield, and fruit from the trees. It is a direct covenantal counterpart to the commentary's source-to-pasture sequence of rain, ground, and provision.

column5: storm clouds, showers, and field vegetation
column6: The LORD makes storm clouds, gives showers of rain, and gives vegetation in the field. It closely matches the page's cloud-to-rain-to-plant chain, including the cloud's first visible role.

column5: seasonal rain before gathered grain, wine, and oil
column6: God gives the early and latter rain so Israel gathers the field's produce. This provides the rain-and-annual-yield side of the pasture provision that the next verse extends to livestock.

column5: Moses's staff at the call
column6: At the call, God asks Moses what is in his hand and he answers, “a staff.” It is the direct Torah counterpart to the commentary's remembered shepherd's staff at the fire.

column5: staff cast down and becoming a serpent
column6: Moses casts the staff down and it becomes a serpent. This supplies the specific transformation noted when the commentary follows the shepherd's staff into the call narrative.

column5: God makes a green tree wither and a dry tree flourish
column6: God declares that he brings down the high tree, makes the green tree wither, and makes the dry tree flourish. Its divine reversal gives a close prophetic counterpart to 87:4–5's brought-forth green turning dark, while retaining renewal as God's act.

column5: command for the dead Lazarus to come out
column6: Jesus calls the dead Lazarus to come out of the tomb. It is a narrative realization of the commentary's second emergence: a dead human is summoned from the place that held him.

column5: sown in decay and raised in incorruption
column6: Paul describes the body as sown in corruption and raised in incorruption. It gives the page's perishing vegetation and more lasting future a direct resurrection contrast.

column5: raised to everlasting life, with a contrary final outcome
column6: A martyr expects God to raise the faithful to everlasting life while denying the persecutor a resurrection to life. It specifically parallels the commentary's move from earthly death to distinct final destinies.

column5: cut tree sprouts again
column6: Job observes that a cut tree still has hope because it can sprout again. The natural recovery image gives a focused Hebrew Bible companion to the commentary's vegetation-based inference that death need not be the final state.

column5: deep things out of darkness brought to light
column6: God uncovers deep things from darkness and brings gloom to light. It makes explicit the hidden-to-visible movement that the commentary hears in pasture emerging from unseen soil.

column5: God's word goes out and accomplishes its purpose
column6: God's word goes out and succeeds in its appointed work. Following the rain-and-sprouting comparison immediately before it, this verse provides a biblical bridge to the commentary's contrast between fading grass and effective instruction.

column5: people of God's pasture and sheep of his hand
column6: In a worship setting, Israel is called the people of God's pasture and the sheep of his hand. It joins praise, divine identity, pasture, and flock in a form particularly close to the commentary's opening “He who” descriptions.

column5: field's seventh-year yield for poor and wild animals
column6: The seventh year's field produce is left so the poor may eat and wild animals take what remains. It gives a concrete Torah form to the commentary's pasture as freely available sustenance rather than a commodity retained by its grower.

column5: forgotten sheaf left for vulnerable neighbors
column6: A forgotten sheaf must remain for the resident alien, orphan, and widow. This is a distinct harvest-share counterpart to the commentary's claim that land's yield bears a due for others.

column5: seedtime and harvest as an unbroken seasonal rhythm
column6: Seedtime and harvest are promised to continue while the earth endures. It supplies the annual rhythm behind the commentary's description of pasture as the year's recurring yield.

column5: water on dry ground and spirit on descendants
column6: God promises water on thirsty ground and streams on dry land, then his spirit on descendants. It explicitly makes physical revival of dry earth the vehicle for a human, spiritual enlargement like the commentary's move from growth to education.

column5: descendants sprout among grass beside watercourses
column6: The recipients of the preceding promise are said to sprout among grass like trees by flowing water. It is a specific biblical use of vegetal emergence to depict a human community's growth.

column5: return to dust
column6: The human returns to the dust from which he was taken. It supplies the first half of the commentary's earth–return–second-emergence pattern, while leaving the later resurrection claim to other texts.

column5: Zipporah given after Moses agrees to dwell with her father
column6: Exodus says Moses agrees to dwell with the Midianite and is then given Zipporah; the commentary's Qur'anic scene makes marriage contingent on a stated term of shepherding labor. The shared Midian sequence is clear, but the terms of the marriage arrangement differ.

column5: tree by water, seasonal fruit, unfading leaf
column6: The Torah-meditating person is like a water-fed tree with seasonal fruit and a leaf that does not wither. It offers a deliberate counter-image to the commentary's temporary pasture and links lasting fruitfulness to received instruction.

column5: idols cannot give rain; the LORD made all
column6: Jeremiah asks whether any false gods can make rain and answers by hoping in the LORD who made all things. It is a precise anti-idolatry-and-provision companion to the commentary's worship question around the one who brings hidden life out.

column5: watered tree stays green in heat and drought
column6: The trusting person is like a tree by water whose leaves stay green and whose fruit does not fail in drought. It gives a biblical counter-pattern to the green pasture that dries, with endurance read through trust.

column5: bones flourish like grass
column6: The restored community's bones flourish like grass as God's hand is made known. This unusually bodily grass image bridges the commentary's vegetal revival with its attention to embodied resurrection.

column5: sprouted seed scorched and withered for lack of root
column6: The sun scorches the sprouted seed and it withers because it has no root. It gives a close specific counterpart to the commentary's green growth that reaches a dry, perishing end.

column5: ripened grain and the harvest
column6: When the grain permits it, the sickle is sent because harvest has come. It adds the completed crop and reaping stage to the page's account of yearly yield and the plant's full course.

column5: farmer waits for precious fruit and seasonal rains
column6: The farmer patiently waits for the earth's valuable fruit through early and latter rains. In its context of awaiting the Lord, it couples the annual crop cycle with expectant eschatological patience.

column5: God supplies seed, bread, and harvest of righteousness
column6: God supplies seed to the sower and bread for food, then increases the harvest of righteousness. It directly joins material produce, gratuitous provision, and the moral growth that the commentary develops from the pasture image.

column5: water of life received without price
column6: The thirsty are invited to take the water of life without cost. It provides an eschatological Christian counterpart to the commentary's theme of life-giving provision and admonition that demand no payment.

column5: the Lamb shepherds and guides to springs of life-water
column6: The Lamb shepherds the redeemed and guides them to springs of living water. It is a Christian eschatological development of the pasture, care, guidance, and enduring-life complex explored in the commentary.

column5: sowing for corruption or eternal life
column6: Sowing to the flesh reaps corruption, while sowing to the Spirit reaps eternal life. The agricultural figure makes the commentary's transient growth and divergent final outcomes into an explicit ethical contrast.

column5: harvest as the end of the age
column6: Jesus identifies the harvest as the end of the age and the reapers as angels. It gives the commentary's annual field imagery an explicitly eschatological culmination without reducing the physical pasture itself to allegory.
